modern:
Look, the month of flowers has come! March winds and April showers have done their work, and the earth is all decked out in beauty. Come, my soul, put on your holiday clothes and go out to gather garlands of heavenly thoughts. You know where to go, for “the beds of spices” are well known to you, and you have so often smelled the perfume of “the sweet flowers” that you’ll go straight to your well-beloved and find all loveliness, all joy in him. That cheek, once so roughly struck with a rod, often wet with tears of sympathy and then defiled with spit, that cheek, as it smiles with mercy, is like fragrant spice to my heart. You didn’t hide your face from shame and spitting, O Lord Jesus, and so I’ll find my dearest delight in praising you. Those cheeks were furrowed by the plow of grief, and streaked crimson with blood from your thorn-crowned forehead. Such marks of boundless love can’t help but charm my soul far more than “pillars of perfume.”

If I can’t see his whole face, I would look at his cheeks, for the smallest glimpse of him is wonderfully refreshing to my spiritual senses and gives a variety of delights. In Jesus I find not only fragrance, but a bed of spices; not one flower, but all kinds of sweet flowers. He is my rose and my lily, my heartsease and my cluster of henna. When he is with me, it’s May all year round, and my soul goes out to wash her happy face in the morning dew of his grace, and to delight herself with the singing of the birds of his promises. Precious Lord Jesus, let me truly know the blessedness that lives in lasting, unbroken fellowship with you. I’m a poor, worthless one whose cheek you have stooped to kiss! Oh, let me kiss you in return with the kisses of my lips.

modern:
Whatever beauty there may be in the material world, Jesus Christ has all of it in the spiritual world ten times over. Among flowers the rose is thought the sweetest, but Jesus is infinitely more beautiful in the garden of the soul than the rose can be in the gardens of earth. He takes first place as the fairest among ten thousand. He is the sun, and all others are the stars; the heavens and the day are dark compared with him, *for the King in his beauty surpasses all*. “I am the rose of *Sharon*.” This was the best and rarest of roses. Jesus isn’t just “the rose”; he is “the rose of Sharon,” just as he calls his righteousness “gold,” and then adds “the gold of Ophir”: the best of the best. He is truly lovely, and lovelier than anything else.

*There is variety in his charms.* The rose delights the eye, and its scent is pleasant and refreshing; in the same way, each of the soul’s senses, whether taste or touch, hearing, sight or spiritual smell, finds its proper satisfaction in Jesus. *Even the memory of his love is sweet.* Take the rose of Sharon, pull it apart petal by petal, and store the petals in the jar of memory, and you’ll find each petal fragrant long afterward, filling the house with perfume. Christ *satisfies the highest taste* of the most cultivated spirit to the full. The greatest lover of perfumes is quite satisfied with the rose; and when the soul has reached her highest level of true taste, she will still be content with Christ; no, she’ll be all the better able to appreciate him. Heaven itself has nothing that surpasses the rose of Sharon. What emblem can fully show his beauty? Human speech and earthly things fail to describe him. Earth’s choicest charms mixed together only faintly picture his overflowing preciousness. Blessed rose, bloom in my heart forever!

modern:
It’s a sweet and blessed event that will come to every believer in God’s own time: going home to be with Jesus. In a few more years the Lord’s soldiers, now fighting “the good fight of faith,” will be done with battle and will have entered into the joy of their Lord. But although Christ prays that his people may eventually be with him where he is, he doesn’t ask that they be taken straight from this world to heaven. He wants them to stay here. Yet how often the weary pilgrim prays, “O that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away and be at rest.” But Christ doesn’t pray like that. He leaves us in his Father’s hands, until, like fully ripe sheaves of grain, we are each gathered into our Master’s barn. Jesus doesn’t plead for us to be removed at once by death, for staying in the body is needed for others, even if it isn’t profitable for ourselves. He asks that we may be kept from evil, but he never asks for us to be admitted to the inheritance in glory until we’re of full age.

Christians often want to die when they have any trouble. Ask them why, and they’ll tell you, “Because we would be with the Lord.” We’re afraid it isn’t so much because they long to be with the Lord as because they want to be rid of their troubles; otherwise they’d feel the same wish to die at other times, when they aren’t under the pressure of trial. They want to go home not so much for the Savior’s company as to be at rest. Now, it’s quite right to desire to depart if we can do it in the same spirit Paul did, because being with Christ is far better; but the wish to escape trouble is a selfish one. Instead, let your care and wish be to glorify God by your life here as long as he pleases, even in the middle of toil and battle and suffering, and leave it to him to say when “it is enough.”

modern: Look at the epitaph of all those blessed saints who fell asleep before our Lord came! It doesn’t matter how else they died, whether of old age or by violence; this one point, which they all share, is the most worth recording: “they all died in faith.” They lived by faith; it was their comfort, their guide, their motive and their support. And in the same spiritual grace they died, ending their life’s song on the sweet note they had kept up so long. They didn’t die resting in the flesh or in their own achievements. They never moved on from the way they were first accepted by God, but held to the way of faith to the end. Faith is as precious to die by as to live by.

Dying in faith looks back to *the past*. They believed the promises that had gone before, and were sure their sins were blotted out through the mercy of God. Dying in faith has to do with *the present*. These saints were confident of their acceptance with God; they enjoyed the beams of his love and rested in his faithfulness. Dying in faith looks into *the future*. They fell asleep declaring that the Messiah would surely come, and that when he appeared on the earth in the last days, they would rise from their graves to see him. To them the pains of death were only the birth pangs of a better state. Take courage, my soul, as you read this epitaph. By grace your course is one of faith, and sight seldom cheers you; this has also been the path of the brightest and best. Faith was the orbit in which these stars of the first magnitude moved all the time they shone here, and you’re happy that it’s yours. Look again tonight to Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith, and thank him for giving you the same precious faith as the souls now in glory.

modern:
Are you asking the reason for this, believer? Look up at your heavenly Father, and see how pure and holy he is. Do you know that one day you’re to be like him? Will you be shaped into his image easily? Won’t you need a great deal of refining in the furnace of affliction to purify you? Will it be easy to get rid of your sinful desires and make you perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect? Next, Christian, turn your eye *downward*. Do you know what enemies you have beneath your feet? You were once a servant of Satan, and no king willingly loses his subjects. Do you think Satan will leave you alone? No, he’ll always be at you, for he “goeth about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” So expect trouble, Christian, when you look beneath you.

Then look *around you*. Where are you? You’re in enemy country, a stranger and a temporary resident. The world isn’t your friend. If it is, then you’re not God’s friend, for whoever is the friend of the world is the enemy of God. You can be sure you’ll find enemies everywhere. When you sleep, think that you’re resting on the battlefield. When you walk, suspect an ambush in every hedge. As mosquitoes are said to bite strangers more than natives, so the trials of earth will be sharpest for you. Last of all, look *within you*, into your own heart, and see what’s there. *Sin* and *self* are still inside. Ah, if you had no devil to tempt you, no enemies to fight you and no world to trap you, you’d still find enough evil in yourself to be a painful trouble to you, for “the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked.” So expect trouble, but don’t lose heart because of it, for God is with you to help and strengthen you. He has said, “I will be with thee in trouble; I will deliver thee and honour thee.”

modern:
Covenant blessings aren’t meant only to be looked at, but to be taken and used. Even our Lord Jesus is given to us for our present use. Believer, you don’t make use of Christ as you ought to. When you’re in trouble, why don’t you tell him all your grief? Doesn’t he have a sympathizing heart, and can’t he comfort and relieve you? No, you go around to all your friends except your best Friend, telling your story everywhere except into the bosom of your Lord. Are you weighed down with today’s sins? Here is a fountain filled with blood: use it, saint, use it. Has a sense of guilt come back on you? The pardoning grace of Jesus can be proved again and again. Come to him at once for cleansing. Are you grieving over your weakness? He is your strength; why not lean on him? Do you feel naked? Come here, soul: put on the robe of Jesus’ righteousness. Don’t stand looking at it; wear it. Strip off your own righteousness, and your own fears too, and put on the fine white linen, for it was meant to be *worn*.

Do you feel sick? Ring the night bell of prayer and wake up the Beloved Physician! He’ll give you the medicine that will revive you. You’re poor, but you have “a kinsman, a mighty man of wealth.” What! Won’t you go to him and ask him to give you some of his abundance, when he has given you this promise, that you’ll be a joint heir with him, and has handed over all that he is and all that he has to be yours? There’s nothing Christ dislikes more than for his people to make a showpiece of him and not use him. He loves to be put to work by us. The more burdens we put on his shoulders, the more precious he’ll be to us.

modern: One great besetting sin of ancient Israel was idolatry, and the spiritual Israel is troubled with a tendency to the same folly. Remphan’s star no longer shines, and the women no longer weep for Tammuz, but Mammon still pushes in his golden calf, and the shrines of pride aren’t abandoned. Self in various forms struggles to bring the chosen under its rule, and the flesh sets up its altars wherever it can find room for them. Favorite children are often the cause of much sin in believers. The Lord is grieved when he sees us doting on them beyond measure. They’ll live to be as great a curse to us as Absalom was to David, or they’ll be taken from us and leave our homes empty. If Christians want to grow thorns to stuff their sleepless pillows, let them dote on their dear ones.

It’s rightly said that “they are no gods,” for the objects of our foolish love are very doubtful blessings. The comfort they give us now is dangerous, and the help they can give in the hour of trouble is very small. So why are we so bewitched with empty things? We pity the poor heathen who worship a god of stone, and yet we worship a god of gold. Where is the great superiority of a god of flesh over one of wood? The principle, the sin, the folly is the same in either case, except that in ours the crime is worse, because we have more light and sin in the face of it. The heathen bows to a false god, but he has never known the true God. We commit two evils, since we forsake the living God and turn to idols. May the Lord cleanse us all from this grievous sin!

modern:
Peter earnestly urged the scattered saints to love each other “with a pure heart fervently,” and he wisely drew his argument not from the law, or nature, or philosophy, but from the high and divine nature God has planted in his people. A wise tutor of princes might work to create and nurture a kingly spirit and dignified behavior in them, finding his arguments in their position and family. In the same way, Peter looks on God’s people as heirs of glory, princes of the royal blood, descendants of the King of kings, earth’s truest and oldest aristocracy, and says to them, “See that ye love one another, because of your noble birth, being born of incorruptible seed; because of your pedigree, being descended from God, the Creator of all things; and because of your immortal destiny, for you shall never pass away, though the glory of the flesh shall fade, and even its existence shall cease.”

It would be good if, in a spirit of humility, we recognized the true dignity of our reborn nature and lived up to it. What is a Christian? Compare him with a king, and he adds priestly holiness to royal dignity. A king’s royalty often lies only in his crown, but with a Christian it is poured into his inmost nature. Through his new birth he is as far above his fellows as a man is above the beast that perishes. Surely he ought to conduct himself in all his dealings as one who isn’t one of the crowd, but chosen out of the world, set apart by sovereign grace, written among “the peculiar people.” So he can’t grovel in the dust like others, or live the way the world’s citizens live. Believers in Christ, let the dignity of your nature and the brightness of your prospects compel you to hold fast to holiness and avoid even the appearance of evil.

notes.note: “Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God” ([[1Pet.1.23|1 Peter 1:23]]). Incorruptible means unable to decay.

modern:
What a sweet title: “My people!” What a cheering revelation: “Their God!” How much meaning is packed into those two words, “My people”! Here is *specialness*. The whole world is God’s; the heaven, even the heaven of heavens, is the Lord’s, and he reigns among the children of men. But of those he has chosen, whom he has bought for himself, he says what he doesn’t say of others: “My people.” In this word there is the idea of *ownership*. In a special way “the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.” All the nations on earth are his; the whole world is in his power; yet his people, his chosen, are more especially his possession, because he has done more for them than for others. He has bought them with his blood. He has brought them near to himself. He has set his great heart on them. He has loved them with an everlasting love, a love that many waters can’t quench, and that the turning of time will never be able to lessen in the least.

Dear friends, can you by faith see yourselves among that number? Can you look up to heaven and say, “My Lord and my God: mine by that sweet *relationship* which entitles me to call thee Father; mine by that hallowed *fellowship* which I delight to hold with thee when thou art pleased to manifest thyself unto me as thou dost not unto the world”? Can you read the inspired Book and find the title deeds of your salvation there? Can you read your title written in precious blood? Can you, by humble faith, take hold of Jesus’ garment and say, “My Christ”? If you can, then God says of you, and of others like you, “My people.” For if God is your God, and Christ your Christ, the Lord has a special, particular favor toward you; you are the object of his choice, accepted in his beloved Son.

modern:
Wisdom is a person’s true strength; under its guidance he best fulfills the purposes of his life. Handling the business of life wisely gives a person the richest enjoyment and the noblest work for his powers, and so through it he finds good in the fullest sense. Without wisdom, a person is like a wild donkey’s colt, running here and there, wasting strength that could be put to good use. Wisdom is the compass by which a person must steer across the trackless waste of life; without it he’s an abandoned ship, the plaything of winds and waves. A person must be wise and careful in a world like this, or he’ll find no good, but be led into countless troubles. The pilgrim will badly wound his feet among the briers in the wood of life if he doesn’t pick his steps with the greatest caution. Anyone in a wilderness full of gangs of robbers must handle things wisely if he wants to travel safely. If, trained by the Great Teacher, we follow where he leads, we’ll find good even in this dark place. There are heavenly fruits to be gathered this side of Eden’s arbors, and songs of paradise to be sung among the groves of earth.

But where will this wisdom be found? Many have dreamed of it but haven’t had it. Where will we learn it? Let’s listen to the voice of the Lord, for he has told the secret. He has shown the sons of men where true wisdom lies, and we have it in the text: “Whoso trusteth in the Lord, happy is he.” *The true way to handle a matter wisely is to trust in the Lord.* This is the sure thread through the most tangled mazes of life; follow it, and find eternal bliss. Whoever trusts in the Lord has a diploma in wisdom granted by inspiration: he is happy now, and he’ll be happier still above. Lord, in this sweet evening, walk with me in the garden and teach me the wisdom of faith.

modern:
Do you want a house for your soul? Do you ask, “What’s the price?” It’s something less than proud human nature will like to give. It’s without money and without price. Ah, you’d like to pay a respectable rent! You’d love to do something to earn Christ? Then you can’t have the house, for it is “without price.” Will you take my Master’s house on a lease for all eternity, with nothing to pay for it, nothing but the ground rent of loving and serving him forever? Will you take Jesus and “dwell in him”? Look, this house is furnished with everything you need. It’s filled with more riches than you’ll spend as long as you live. Here you can have close fellowship with Christ and feast on his love. Here are tables well stocked with food for you to live on forever. In it, when you’re tired, you can find rest with Jesus, and from it you can look out and see heaven itself.

Will you have the house? Ah, if you’re homeless, you’ll say, “I should like to have the house; but may I have it?” Yes; there’s the key, and the key is “Come to Jesus.” “But,” you say, “I am too shabby for such a house.” Never mind; there are clothes inside. If you feel guilty and condemned, come; and though the house is too good for you, Christ will make you good enough for the house before long. He’ll wash you and clean you, and you’ll yet be able to sing, “We dwell in him.” Believer, how very happy you are to have such a home! You’re greatly privileged, for you have a “strong habitation” where you’re always safe. And “dwelling in him,” you have not only a perfect and secure house, but an *everlasting* one. When this world has melted like a dream, our house will live on and stand, more lasting than marble, more solid than granite, self-existent as God, for it is God himself: “We dwell in him.”

notes.note: “Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit” ([[1John.4.13|1 John 4:13]]).

modern:
*A short stay on earth will make heaven more heavenly.* Nothing makes rest so sweet as toil; nothing makes safety so pleasant as being exposed to alarm. The bitter quassia cups of earth will add relish to the new wine that sparkles in the golden bowls of glory. Our battered armor and scarred faces will make our victory above more glorious, when we’re welcomed to the seats of those who have overcome the world. We wouldn’t have full *fellowship with Christ* if we didn’t live here below for a while, for he was baptized with a baptism of suffering among men, and we must be baptized with the same if we want to share his kingdom. Fellowship with Christ is so honorable that the sharpest sorrow is a small price to pay for it. Another reason we linger here is *for the good of others*. We wouldn’t want to enter heaven until our work is done, and it may be that we’re still appointed to bring light to souls lost in darkness in the wilderness of sin.

No doubt our long stay here is also *for God’s glory*. A tested saint, like a well-cut diamond, sparkles brightly in the King’s crown. Nothing brings so much honor to a workman as a long, hard test of his work, which it comes through in triumph without giving way anywhere. We are God’s workmanship, and he will be glorified in us by our afflictions. It’s for the honor of Jesus that we endure the testing of our faith with holy joy. Let each of us give up our own longings to the glory of Jesus, and feel, “If my lying in the dust would elevate my Lord by so much as an inch, let me still lie among the pots of earth. If to live on earth for ever would make my Lord more glorious, it should be my heaven to be shut out of heaven.” Our time is fixed and settled by eternal decree. Let’s not be anxious about it, but wait patiently until the gates of pearl open.

modern: What a mass of hideous sickness must have been pushed in front of Jesus’ eyes! Yet we don’t read that he was disgusted; he patiently attended to every case. What a strange variety of ills must have gathered at his feet! What sickening ulcers and rotting sores! Yet he was ready for every new shape of that monster, evil, and conquered it in every form. Let the arrow fly from wherever it might, he put out its fiery power. The heat of fever or the cold of dropsy, the stupor of palsy or the rage of madness, the filth of leprosy or the darkness of eye disease: all felt the power of his word and fled at his command. In every corner of the field he triumphed over evil and received the homage of freed captives. He came, he saw, he conquered everywhere. It’s the same this morning. Whatever my own case may be, the beloved Physician can heal me; and whatever the state of others I may remember in prayer right now, I can hope in Jesus that he’ll be able to heal them of their sins. My child, my friend, my dearest one: I can have hope for each, for all, when I remember my Lord’s healing power. And for my own part, however hard my struggle with sins and weaknesses, I can still be of good cheer. He who walked the hospitals on earth still gives out his grace and works wonders among the sons of men. Let me go to him at once, in real earnest.

Let me praise him this morning as I remember how he worked his spiritual cures, which bring him the most fame. It was by taking our sicknesses on himself. “By his stripes we are healed.” The church on earth is full of souls healed by our beloved Physician, and the people of heaven itself confess that “He healed them all.” Come, then, my soul, spread abroad the power of his grace, and let it be “to the Lord for a name, for an everlasting sign which shall not be cut off.”

modern: Like many others, the disabled man had been waiting for a wonder to happen and a sign to be given. Wearily he watched the pool, but no angel came, or none came for him. Yet thinking it was his only chance, he kept waiting, and didn’t know that there was One near him whose word could heal him in a moment. Many are in the same plight. They’re waiting for some unusual emotion, some remarkable impression or heavenly vision; they wait in vain and watch for nothing. Even supposing remarkable signs are seen in a few cases, they’re rare, and no one has a right to look for them in his own case; especially no one who feels he’s too weak to make use of the moving of the water even if it came. It’s a very sad thought that tens of thousands are waiting right now in the use of means and ordinances and vows and resolutions, and have waited like this for ages, in vain, completely in vain. Meanwhile these poor souls forget the Savior who is here now, who tells them to look to him and be saved. He could heal them at once, but they’d rather wait for an angel and a wonder. Trusting him is the sure way to every blessing, and he deserves the most complete confidence; but unbelief makes them prefer the cold porches of Bethesda to the warm bosom of his love. Oh, that the Lord may turn his eye on the crowds who are in this state tonight! May he forgive the slights they put on his divine power, and call them by that sweet, compelling voice to rise from the bed of despair and, in the energy of faith, take up their bed and walk. O Lord, hear our prayer for all such people at this calm hour of sunset, and before the day breaks may they look and live.
Kind reader, is there anything in this reading for you?
